items.stem: A team wants the model to know this week's prices, which change constantly. Why is fine-tuning a poor fit?

options.text: Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights and cannot be cheaply updated each week; retrieval keeps changing facts current
options.rationale: Correct: volatile facts belong in retrieval, not in fine-tuned weights.

options.text: Fine-tuning can never change model behaviour
options.rationale: It can change behaviour; the issue is updating volatile facts.

options.text: Prices cannot be represented as text
options.rationale: They can; the problem is update frequency.

options.text: Fine-tuning is always cheaper than retrieval
options.rationale: For frequently changing data, re-tuning is costly, not cheaper.

items.explanation: Correct: volatile facts belong in retrieval, not in fine-tuned weights.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which TWO are advantages of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g. LoRA) over full fine-tuning? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Lower compute and memory cost to train
options.rationale: Correct: only a small set of added parameters is trained.

options.text: Smaller artefacts that are easier to store and swap
options.rationale: Correct: adapters are small compared with full model copies.

options.text: It guarantees higher accuracy than full fine-tuning in all cases
options.rationale: It does not guarantee higher accuracy; it trades some capacity for efficiency.

options.text: It removes the need for any training data

items.explanation: Correct: only a small set of added parameters is trained.

items.stem: Training loss keeps falling but validation loss starts rising. What does this indicate?

options.text: Overfitting: the model is memorising the training set and generalising worse
options.rationale: Correct: a widening train/validation gap is the classic overfitting signal.

options.text: The dataset is too small to train at all
options.rationale: Training loss is improving, so training is happening; the issue is generalisation.
A zero learning rate would not lower training loss.
Rising validation loss means it should stop earlier, not that it succeeded.

items.explanation: Correct: a widening train/validation gap is the classic overfitting signal.
